$comment: The nine leak cards (L1 to L9): how a secret stays readable in a .NET process. Each card is stored once, here, and rendered by LeakCard.astro under a pin, on /concepts/how-secrets-leak/ and in a memory strip's captions. A title has at most six words and a body at most 80. Evidence names a key of evidence.json's tests, samples, sources or external. Text fields take `code` and [links](/x/).

leaks.title: The collector moves arrays
leaks.body: A collection can compact the heap: it copies the objects still in use to new addresses, an array that holds a key among them. Microsoft's page on `SecureString` says that, because a string's memory is not pinned, the collector "will make additional copies" of it when it moves and compacts memory. Which objects move, and when, is the collector's decision.
leaks.verdictText: For the buffers it allocates: they are pinned, and the collector does not move them. Stack memory does not move either. It does not help with heap memory you already had.
leaks.mechanism: Allocation on the pinned object heap

leaks.title: Freed is not erased
leaks.body: When nothing references an array any more, the collector takes its memory back without overwriting it, and nothing clears an array when your method returns. A crash dump or a page file can hold those bytes until the memory is used again, and an allocation that skips zeroing, as `GC.AllocateUninitializedArray` does, can be handed them as they are.
leaks.verdictText: `Dispose` overwrites the buffer with zeros before the memory is let go. It does nothing for a buffer you never dispose, and a new buffer is not cleared for you: write before you read.

leaks.title: Pools pass your bytes on
leaks.body: `ArrayPool<T>.Return` leaves the array as it is unless you pass `clearArray: true`, and the next `Rent` can hand that array to another caller, who reads what you left in it. `MemoryPool<T>.Shared`, and `BufferFactory.Rent` with `isSensitive: false`, rent from the same kind of pool.
leaks.verdictText: With `isSensitive: true`: `Dispose` overwrites the buffer with zeros before the pool can rent it out again.

leaks.title: Growing makes copies
leaks.body: A buffer that grows, such as `ArrayBufferWriter<T>`, `MemoryStream` or `List<T>`, allocates a larger array and copies what it holds into it. The smaller array is dropped with the first part of your secret still in it, and nothing clears it.
leaks.verdictText: The pooled buffer writer adds a segment instead of copying: nothing already written is moved or dropped.

leaks.title: Strings cannot be erased
leaks.body: A `string` cannot be changed after it is made, so your code cannot overwrite it, and the collector frees it when it chooses. Every `GetString`, `ToBase64String`, interpolation or deserialized property makes one more.
leaks.verdictText: Nothing reaches a string that already exists. The guides read and decode a secret into a buffer, so that no string of it is made.

leaks.title: An exception skips your cleanup
leaks.body: A `Clear` or `ZeroMemory` call written after the work runs only when the work finishes. An exception or an early `return` leaves the method before that line, and the secret stays where it was.
leaks.verdictText: When you write `using`: the owner is disposed on every way out of the block, an exception included. That is C#'s rule, and the library's owners are `IDisposable` so that you can use it.

leaks.title: An early exit tells time
leaks.body: A comparison that stops at the first difference, such as `==`, `SequenceEqual` or a loop of your own, returns sooner the earlier two values differ. Someone who can send many guesses and time the answers can learn an expected MAC one byte at a time.
leaks.verdictText: For values of the same length: `FixedTimeEquals` calls .NET's fixed-time comparison. The length still shows.

leaks.title: A lenient decoder invents characters
leaks.body: `Encoding.UTF8` and `Encoding.ASCII` replace bytes they cannot decode with a substitute character. Two different inputs can then decode to the same string, so the bytes you checked are not the text you used.
leaks.verdictText: `SecureEncoding` throws on invalid input instead of substituting.

leaks.title: Copies are on their own
leaks.body: `ToArray()`, `Convert.ToBase64String`, a `string`, an array an API keeps: each copy of a secret is new memory. Disposing the original writes zeros to the original only.
leaks.verdictText: Nothing reaches a copy. The guides show how to do the work without making one.
